workbookTitle: Learn programming with the embroidery machine – turtle previews
S0E1I1: Our goal is to decorate a shopping bag with embroidery ourselves. The workshop is divided into two parts.
S0E1I2: Sections 1–6 cover patterns, loops, custom blocks, counters, conditionals and recursion. Programming tasks have an interactive turtle preview and are completed directly in this workbook. Existing TurtleStitch projects remain available for download and exploration.
S0E1I3: In the second part we create a pattern ourselves that we embroider into the bag. Here we use the techniques we learned before. You have the last hour of the workshop to do this!

S7E1I1: Now use your creativity (PDF task 6): design your own single-colour pattern in the editor. Use loops, functions, parameters and, where helpful, conditions or recursion. This task has no prescribed target pattern.
S7E1I2: In order for the pattern to be embroidered, it must meet the following properties:
S7E1I3:
1. At most 20 × 20 cm on the fabric.
  2. One colour only (black, red, green or blue).
  3. Suitable stitch spacing; the turtle preview checks geometry, not embroidery suitability.
S7E1I4: Your program is saved in the workbook. For production, transfer it to TurtleStitch and save the project there. Check scale, stitch spacing and the machine format with a supervisor before embroidering.
S5Modulo: `i modulo 2` (in Python: `i % 2`) is the remainder when dividing i by 2. Enter the remainder for i = 1 through 7. Which remainders occur for even and odd numbers?
S5Predict: Predict before running: a program counts i from 1 to 6. If `i % 2 == 0`, it draws a triangle; otherwise it draws a square. It then moves to the next position with the pen up. What sequence do you expect?
S5Example: Open the editor and inspect the supplied program. It draws six shapes with side length 40, with starting points 80 steps apart. Change the condition to `i % 2 == 1`. What changes? Then restore the original pattern.
S5Explain: Explain what `if … else …` does and why `i % 2 == 0` recognizes even numbers. Compare the result with your prediction.
S5Alternate: Draw eleven shapes: odd positions contain a house (square and roof, both side length 30); even positions contain an upward-pointing equilateral triangle of side length 60. Starting points are x = 0, 80, …, 800 at y = 0. Use a loop and a condition.
S5EveryFourth: Change the pattern: only every fourth shape is a large triangle; the others are small houses. Use `i % 4`. Keep the same sizes and starting points.
S5Reflect: Which condition did you choose? What would you change so that only every third shape is a triangle?
S6Introduction: Recursion means that a function calls itself. The Koch function from PDF task 5a draws a 50-step line at level 0. Otherwise it calls itself four times with `level - 1`, turning left 60°, right 120° and left 60° between calls. Negative `turn` angles turn left; positive angles turn right.
S6Run: Open the editor, read the supplied `koch(level)` function and run it at level 0. Find the base case and recursive calls.
S6Predict: Predict how the number of segments and overall width change at levels 1, 2 and 3. Why does the function terminate?
S6Levels: Recreate the four previews using the function from 6a (PDF task 5b). The smallest segment always remains 50 steps long, so the widths are 50, 150, 450 and 1350 steps. Each curve starts at (0, 0), facing right. Compare the results with your prediction.
S6Length: Add a `length` parameter (PDF task 5c). All curves should be 270 steps wide. Hint: divide the length by 3 at each recursive call. The base case moves forward by the supplied length.
S6LengthExplain: Explain why you divide by 3 even though there are four recursive calls. How long is the smallest segment at level 3?
S6Snowflake: Extend your program to a snowflake (PDF task 5d). Draw three Koch curves of overall length 270, turning right 120° between them. Start at (0, 0), facing right. Create snowflakes at levels 0 through 3.
S6Branches: Recreate the branching star from PDF task 5e. Draw six branches from the origin, turning 60° between them. A branch moves forward 90 steps; at its tip, three smaller branches turn left 60°, go straight and turn right 60°. Divide length by 3 each time and branch until level 0 (start level 2). Return to the start of each branch with the pen up so no segment is stitched twice.
S6Termination: Describe your star’s base case. What happens without a base case? Explain how your program restores position and direction after each branch.
S7DesignReflection: Which techniques did you use? Describe how to adjust the size and spacing of your pattern.
S7Ready: Scale, colour and stitch spacing checked with a supervisor.
S5NestedPredict: The next program counts i from 0 to 10 and checks i modulo 3. Remainder 0 draws a triangle; otherwise a second condition checks for remainder 1 to draw a square, or a triangle for other remainders. Predict the sequence before running it.
S5NestedRun: Inspect the supplied program from PDF task 4d in the editor. Shapes have side length 25; starting points are 50 steps apart. Compare the result with your prediction.
S5NestedExplain: Why is the second condition checked only inside the else branch? Which remainders can i modulo 3 have, and when does each branch run?
